baseline: Host LTP 20260529 (kernel 6.8.0-124-generic): 1 passed / 0 failed / 0 broken. setup() reads /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max = 4194304; the single assertion wait402.c:23 calls wait4(4194305, &status, 0, &rusage) and the correct kernel returns -1/ECHILD (10) because 4194305 is an ordinary positive pid_t that simply matches no child of the caller. Direct host syscall probe of the surrounding boundary (/tmp/w4probe.c) pins down which inputs are special and which are not: wait4(4194305) -> ECHILD, wait4(INT_MAX=2147483647) -> ECHILD, wait4(-2) -> ECHILD, wait4(2147483648) -> ESRCH (the value truncates to INT_MIN in the i32 argument), wait4(INT_MIN) -> ESRCH. So ESRCH is correct for exactly one pid value, INT_MIN, and ECHILD is correct for every other non-matching pid including INT_MAX. The rule the baseline establishes is therefore not about wait4 at all: a conforming kernel advertises a pid_max low enough that pid_max + 1 is still a representable positive pid_t, which is what makes the ECHILD path reachable.
failing_assertion: wait402.c:23: TFAIL: wait4(pid_max + 1, &status, 0, &rusage) expected ECHILD: ESRCH (3). Asterinas returns ESRCH (3) where the correct value is ECHILD (10). Captured from qemu.log line 53 of the KIRK_VERBOSE=1 boot; the default non-verbose runner only reports 'wait402: fail (0.012s)' with passed 0 / failed 1 / broken 0, and the broken count of 0 is itself evidence that setup()'s SAFE_FILE_SCANF of /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max succeeded and the failure is the assertion proper, not a missing procfs file.
root_cause: PID_MAX is defined as `pub const PID_MAX: u32 = u32::MAX / 2` at kernel/src/process/posix_thread/mod.rs:425, and u32::MAX / 2 is exactly 2147483647 = i32::MAX. kernel/src/fs/fs_impls/procfs/sys/kernel/pid_max.rs:29 prints that constant verbatim into /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max, so the guest advertises a pid_max of i32::MAX. The test reads it into a pid_t and computes pid_max + 1 = 2147483648, which does not fit in the signed 32-bit pid_t that wait4 takes, so it arrives at the syscall as the bit pattern 0x80000000. sys_wait4 (kernel/src/syscall/wait4.rs:25) casts the raw u64 argument to i32, yielding i32::MIN, and hands it to ProcessFilter::from_id (kernel/src/process/process_filter.rs:49-72), whose first arm at lines 53-55 special-cases wait_pid == i32::MIN and returns ESRCH because negating it would overflow. That arm is correct and matches Linux exactly; it fires here only because the advertised pid_max was large enough that pid_max + 1 overflowed into it. The generic ECHILD machinery it never reaches is present and correct at kernel/src/process/wait.rs:81-86, which returns ECHILD once neither try_wait_tracees nor try_wait_children matches. So no wait4 code is wrong: the single wrong value is the PID_MAX constant, whose own FIXME at lines 422-424 states the value was chosen arbitrarily.
invariant: The maximum process ID a kernel advertises must leave headroom above itself inside the signed pid_t that the wait and kill syscalls accept: pid_max + 1 must still be a representable positive pid_t, so that a caller can name an unallocated PID and get the not-my-child answer (ECHILD) rather than tripping the sign-overflow guard (ESRCH). Setting pid_max to the largest positive pid_t makes the value one past the ceiling unnameable and silently reclassifies it as a process-group query. Separately, whatever ceiling the PID allocator enforces and the value /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max reports must be the same number, since userspace sizes its PID arithmetic from the latter.
owning_layer: The PID allocation policy layer that owns the PID_MAX ceiling: kernel/src/process/posix_thread/mod.rs (the PID_MAX constant at line 425, consumed by allocate_posix_tid at 401-414 and re-exported to the procfs sysctl). This is the layer that must be corrected, not the wait4 path. ProcessFilter::from_id and sys_wait4 are both already right, so a narrower edit at the syscall layer, such as relaxing the i32::MIN arm to return ECHILD, would make this one test green while breaking genuine conformance: the host probe shows real Linux does return ESRCH for wait4(INT_MIN), so that edit would trade a correct behavior away for an incorrect one. Asterinas's structure lines up with Linux's here (a compile-time ceiling consulted by the allocator and reported through a procfs sysctl), so no abstraction mismatch needs resolving; only the constant's value diverges.
linux_reference: Two places, both read on the web. (1) The ceiling: include/linux/threads.h defines PID_MAX_LIMIT as (sizeof(long) > 4 ? 4 * 1024 * 1024 : PID_MAX_DEFAULT), i.e. 4194304 on 64-bit, with the comment 'A maximum of 4 million PIDs should be enough for a while. [NOTE: PID/TIDs are limited to 2^30 ~= 1 billion, see FUTEX_TID_MASK.]' PID_MAX_DEFAULT is 0x8000 (32768) unless CONFIG_BASE_SMALL. So Linux deliberately keeps its ceiling three orders of magnitude below i32::MAX, and even its hard architectural bound is 2^30, still well clear of the sign boundary; the host's observed pid_max of 4194304 is PID_MAX_LIMIT reached via pid_idr_init scaling by CPU count in kernel/pid.c. That headroom is what makes pid_max + 1 a normal positive pid on Linux. (2) The guard Asterinas mirrors: kernel_wait4 in kernel/exit.c rejects the one unnegatable input up front, after options validation and before any pid lookup, with `/* -INT_MIN is not defined */ if (upid == INT_MIN) return -ESRCH;` followed by the -1 / <0 / ==0 / >0 branches. Asterinas's ProcessFilter::from_id is arm-for-arm the same function including that ESRCH, which is the strongest evidence the wait4 side needs no change. Note waitid has no such check because it never negates upid, matching from_which_and_id.
other_callers: PID_MAX has two other consumers in-tree, both of which inherit the wrong ceiling from the same constant. kernel/src/fs/fs_impls/procfs/sys/kernel/pid_max.rs:29 is the reporting path this test observes, so every userspace program that sizes PID arithmetic or a PID bitmap from /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max is handed i32::MAX today; anything allocating a table of that many entries, as ps and monitoring tools do, is affected far beyond this test. kernel/src/fs/fs_impls/cgroupfs/controller/pids.rs:114 validates writes to cgroup pids.max against PID_MAX, so it currently accepts absurd limits up to i32::MAX. Beyond PID_MAX's own callers, the ESRCH-instead-of-ECHILD symptom is reachable through every syscall that takes a signed pid and is documented to report ECHILD or ESRCH for an unmatched one: ProcessFilter::from_id is shared by sys_wait4 and sys_kill per its own comment at process_filter.rs:48, so kill(pid_max + 1, sig) misreports on the same arithmetic. allocate_posix_tid (mod.rs:401-414) only warns when it crosses PID_MAX and still returns the tid, so lowering the constant changes no allocation behavior at any reachable thread count; the FIXME there about being unable to recycle smaller PIDs is a pre-existing gap that this fix neither closes nor worsens.
suggested_direction: Change PID_MAX at kernel/src/process/posix_thread/mod.rs:425 from `u32::MAX / 2` to Linux's 64-bit PID_MAX_LIMIT, 4 * 1024 * 1024 = 4194304, and replace the 'chosen arbitrarily' FIXME at lines 422-424 with a reference to include/linux/threads.h so the value's provenance is recorded. This restores the headroom the invariant requires: pid_max + 1 = 4194305 stays a positive pid_t, from_id takes the final else arm at process_filter.rs:68-71 and builds ProcessFilter::WithPid(4194305), wait.rs:81-86 finds no matching child or tracee, and wait4 returns ECHILD. Touch neither process_filter.rs nor wait4.rs; both already match kernel_wait4, and the i32::MIN ESRCH arm in particular must be preserved because real Linux returns ESRCH there. Check the two other PID_MAX consumers still behave: the procfs read is a plain reprint and needs no change, and the cgroupfs pids.max bound at pids.rs:114 simply tightens. Verify with the default configuration and an empty run_vars, since the pool entry is in all.txt and needs no workdir override; the enable action is uncommenting all.txt line 1819. Worth probing waitpid01 (all.txt:1822, still commented and unprobed) in the same boot, as it may share the pid_max dependency and come green for free.
